Surah al-Infitar (The Cleaving)

It is also called Surat Infatarat and Surat al-Munfatirah. There is no disagreement that it is Meccan, nor that it has nineteen verses, and its connection to what precedes it is well known.

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿When the sky is cleaved asunder﴾, i.e., split open for the descent of the angels, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And the day the sky will be split open with clouds, and the angels will be sent down, descending﴾. The discussion concerning the raising of the sky is as was mentioned concerning the raising of the sun.

﴿And when the stars are scattered﴾, i.e., they fall, dispersed. This is a metaphor (isti'arah) for their removal, in that they are likened to pearls whose string has been cut; it is either an explicit (musarrahah) or an implicit (makniyyah) metaphor.

When the seas are made to overflow (﴿وإذا البِحارُ فُجِّرَتْ﴾): they are opened up and their sides split, so the barrier (al-barzakh) between them disappears, the sweet and the salty mix together, and they become one single sea. It is also narrated that the earth drinks up the water after the seas have filled, so that it becomes level, meaning that there is no water left. The intended meaning is that the seas first become one, then the earth dries up entirely and becomes without water. It is also possible that what is meant by levelness after the drying up is that no hollows of water remain, in accordance with His saying, exalted is He: ﴿لا تَرى فِيها عِوَجًا ولا أمْتًا﴾ ("You will see no crookedness or unevenness in it").

Mujahid, al-Rabi' ibn Khaytham, al-Za'farani and al-Thawri read "fujirat" (فُجِرَتْ) with a light vowelling, in the passive voice. It is also reported from Mujahid that he read "fajarat" (فَجَرَتْ) with a fatha on the fa and in the active voice, meaning "gushed forth," because the barrier disappears through debauchery (al-fujur), looking to His saying, exalted is He: ﴿لا يَبْغِيانِ﴾ ("they do not transgress"), since transgression (al-baghy) and debauchery (al-fujur) are brothers.

﴿And when the graves are overturned﴾. It means that the dust of the graves, which had been heaped over their dead, is turned over, scattered, and removed, and those buried in them are brought out, as some commentators have explained. The root of *ba'thara* (to overturn or scatter), it is said, is the scattering of dust or the like, and this happens only to bring out something beneath it. It may therefore be mentioned while both its meaning and its necessary implication are intended together, and the meaning you have heard is intended as well. It is also sometimes used figuratively for raising and bringing out, as in the verse about the charging steeds (*al-'adiyat*), where the act is attributed to what is in the graves rather than to the graves themselves, as here. Some have claimed that it is a homonym meaning both digging up and bringing out. Some scholars, such as al-Zamakhshari and al-Suhayli, held that it is a compound of two words, abbreviated, and this is called *naht* (word-blending). The origin of *bu'thira* is *bu'itha* (was raised) and *uthira* (was stirred up). Its parallels are *basmala* (to say "in the name of Allah"), *hamdala* (to say "praise be to Allah"), *hawqala* (to say "there is no power nor strength except in Allah, exalted is He"), and *damʿaza* (to say "may Allah perpetuate his might"), along with other such examples, which are numerous in the Arabic language. On this view its meaning is digging up and bringing out together. Abu Hayyan objected that *ra'* is not among the letters of augmentation, but this is his own error, for he distinguished between composition (*tarkib*) and blending two words, and between augmentation of some original letters within a single word, as he set out in *al-Zahr*, quoting the lexicographers. Indeed, the default assumption is that there is no composition.

﴿Every soul will know what it has put forward and what it has left behind.﴾ This is the answer (jawab) to «إذا» (idha, "when"). However, it is not that the soul knows this at the Resurrection (al-ba'th). Rather, it knows it at the unfolding of the scrolls (nashr al-suhuf), since the intended meaning of the time is a single period. Its beginning is shortly before the first blast of the Trumpet, or the blast itself, and its end is the separation between creatures (al-fasl bayn al-khala'iq). It is not multiple periods according to the word «إذا». The word is repeated only to magnify the calamities contained within its scope, and what is said about it is like what has passed concerning its counterpart.

The meaning of «ما قَدَّمَ وأخَّرَ» (what one has put forward and left behind) is: what one has sent ahead of deeds of good or evil, and what one has left behind of a good or evil sunnah (practice) that is acted upon after him. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn Mas'ud. It is also reported from Ibn 'Abbas that it means: what one has put forward of disobedience and left behind of obedience, and this is the view of Qatada. It has also been said: what one has done of what one was obligated to do, and what one has not done of it. It has been said: what one has put forward of one's wealth for oneself, and what one has left behind for one's heirs. And it has been said: the first of one's deeds and the last of them. The meaning of the soul's knowledge of both is its detailed knowledge (al-'ilm al-tafsili), as mentioned concerning what came earlier.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 82, verse 6:

﴿O humankind, what has deceived you concerning your Lord, the Most Generous?﴾ That is: what thing deceived you and emboldened you to disobey Him, the Exalted, and to commit what does not befit His majesty, mighty is His majesty. You know what lies before you and what of your deeds will manifest against you, and [you know that] confronting the title of His generosity, exalted is He, rather than His overpowering might, glorified is He, from the attributes of majesty whose consideration would prevent deception, [is a sign] that this [generosity] is not something fit to be the ground of your deception, in accordance with what Satan seduces you with, saying to you: "Do what you will, for your Lord is generous; He has bestowed favour upon you in this world, and He will do the like in the Hereafter." Or he says to him something similar to that, whose foundation is generosity, like the saying of one of the devils of mankind:

"Multiply your sins as much as you are able; tomorrow you will meet a Lord who is Forgiving."

"You will bite your hands in regret for what you left of pleasure out of fear of sin."

This is barren analogy and vain wishful thinking. Rather, it is among those things that necessitate intensifying the turning toward faith and obedience and abstaining from disbelief and disobedience, not the reverse. For this reason, one of the knowers of God said: "If I did not fear God, the Exalted, I would not disobey Him." It is as if it were said: "What has moved you to disobey your Lord, who is described by that which restrains from it and calls to its opposite?" It has also been said: this is a prompting of the proof, and it is also from His generosity, for when it is said to him, "What has deceived you?" etc., he will perceive the answer that was suggested to him and say: "His generosity," as it has been said: "The goodness of character and kindness are known by the scarcity of manners in boys." Zamakhshari did not approve of this, and the deception by it is in the lofty view; otherwise, in the fine view, it is as you have heard. And from al-Fudayl that he said: "His concealment, which is lengthened, deceived him." Muhammad ibn al-Sammak said:

"O you who conceal your sin, are you not ashamed, while God sees you in privacy?

What deceived you concerning your Lord is His respite toward you and His covering of your evil deeds for so long."

Some of them said:

"My Master says, 'Are you not ashamed of what I see of your bad deeds?'

So I said: 'O my Master, be gentle, for the abundance of Your bounties has emboldened me.'"

Qatada said: "His enemy, who was given power over him, deceived him."

It is related that the Prophet (ﷺ) recited the verse and said: "Ignorance."

Umar (may Allah be pleased with him) also said this, and he recited: ﴿Indeed, he was a wrongdoer, ignorant.﴾ The difference between this and what they mentioned is not hidden from one of knowledge. Regarding "al-Insan" (the human being) addressed, it was said: it is the disbeliever; indeed, from Ikrimah it is related that he is Ubayy ibn Khalaf. It was said: it is the more general, encompassing the disobedient, and this is the view due to the generality of the wording, and due to its occurring between the summary and its detail, I mean: ﴿A soul will know﴾ and ﴿Indeed, the righteous﴾ and ﴿Indeed, the wicked﴾. As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Nay, you deny the Judgment﴾, in al-Kashf it is said: either it is an intensification of the strength of their deception, by giving the impression that they are in a worse state than the deniers, as an intensification, or it is for the validity of addressing all with what is found among them. Ibn Jubayr and al-A'mash read: "ma agharak" with a hamza; it is possible that it is an exclamation, and that "ma" is interrogative as in the reading of the majority, and "agharak" means "caused you to fall into heedlessness."

The words of Allah, glorified is He: ﴿Who created you, then proportioned you, then balanced you﴾ are a second attribute, confirming lordship (ruboobiyyah), showing His generosity, alluding to the truth of what they denied concerning resurrection and recompense, and preparing for what follows, since it draws attention to the fact that whoever is able to originate creation is more able to bring it back again. Taswiyah (proportioning) means making the limbs upright, sound, and prepared for their benefits. In origin it means making things equal (sawa'), so that they are in accordance with wisdom and its requirements, by giving each thing that by which it is completed, and balancing (ʿadl) some of them with others so that they are made equitable, from the expression "ʿadala fulānan bi-fulān" when one makes two equal. Or it means turning them away from a form that is not suitable for them, from "ʿadala" in the sense of "ṣaraf" (to turn away). Al-Farisi took the first view, and al-Farra' the second. Several of the Seven Readers read ﴿ʿaddalaka﴾ with shaddah; that is, He made you balanced, proportionate in creation, without any disharmony in it. Al-Qaffal related from some of them that ʿadala and ʿaddala have one meaning.

*"In whatever form He willed, He assembled you"* (﴿فِي أيِّ صُورَةٍ ما شاءَ رَكَّبَكَ﴾): i.e., He assembled you and placed you in whatever form His will and His wisdom, exalted is He, required from among the different forms, varying in height and shortness, degrees of beauty, and the like. The prepositional phrase (al-jarr wa'l-majrur, the prepositional phrase) is connected to *rakkabaka* ("assembled you"), and *ayy* ("whatever") is a qualifier (ṣifah, adjectival modifier) like it in the poet's saying:

*"Have you seen what temples and cheeks appeared to us between al-Liwa and Zarud?"*

Since generality is intended, the thing it qualifies is not mentioned. The clause *shā'a* ("He willed") is a qualifier of it, its returning pronoun is omitted, and *mā* is superfluous (mazīdah, extra). The clause was not joined by a conjunction to what precedes it because it is an explanation of *'adalaka* ("proportioned you").

It is also permitted that the prepositional phrase be in the position of a circumstantial state (ḥāl); that is, "He assembled you being in whatever form He willed." It was also said that *ayy* is a relative (mawṣūlah) whose relative clause is the clause *shā'aha* ("He willed it"), as if it were said: "He assembled you in the form that He willed."

Abu 'Ali [al-Farisi] stated in *al-Tadhkirah* that the relative *ayy* is not annexed to an indefinite noun. Ibn Malik said in the *Alfiyyah*:

*"Specify relative ayy with definiteness."*

In al-Suyuti's commentary on it, along with the condition mentioned above, meaning that the definite noun is not singular, "do not annex it to an indefinite noun," differing from Ibn 'Usfur.

It is also permitted that *ayy* be made a conditional (shartiyyah, conditional particle), and the past tense verb in its response is in the sense of the future, when one considers the connection of the will and the consequence of the assembling. So the past form *shā'aha* is used with regard to the will, and the conditional particle is used with regard to the connection and the consequence. It is also permitted that the prepositional phrase be connected to *'adalaka* ("proportioned you"). In that case *ayy* must be a qualifier, as if it were said: "He proportioned you in the form of whatever form, in a wondrous form," and then the qualified noun was deleted for the sake of magnification and wonder. This *ayy* is transferred from the interrogative (istifhamiyyah, interrogative) use, but its meaning has been completely stripped from it, so the preceding word governs it. The phrase *"mā shā'a rakkabaka"* ("whatever He willed, He assembled you") is then a resumed statement (kalam mustaʾnaf, new sentence). *Mā* may be either a relative or a descriptive (mawṣūfah) and either a subject (mubtada', subject of a nominal sentence) or an absolute object (mafʿūl muṭlaq, cognate object) of *rakkabaka*; that is: "whatever of assembling He willed, He assembled you in it," or "an assembling He willed, He assembled you." It is also permitted that it be conditional, with *shā'a* as the conditional verb and *rakkabaka* as its response: "if He willed to assemble you in whatever form other than this form, He would assemble you in it." The conditional clause is in the position of a qualifier to *ṣūrah*, and the returning pronoun is omitted. They did not permit, on this view, that the adverbial phrase be connected to *rakkabaka*, because the complement of *mā* within the scope of the condition may not be placed before it.

﴿Kalla﴾ is a rebuke against being deceived by the generosity of God, Exalted is He, and against making it a means to disbelief and sins, although it should be a cause for gratitude and obedience. His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿Nay, but you deny the Judgment﴾, is a turning away from an implied clause to which the discourse leads. It is as if it were said after the rebuke, by way of parenthetical digression: "And you do not refrain from that. Rather, you are bold enough to commit something greater than it, in that you deny the recompense and the resurrection outright, or the religion of Islam, which is among the things it commands. So you do not believe in a question, nor an answer, nor a reward, nor a punishment." In this there is a progression from the lesser to the greater.

From al-Raghib (al-Raghib al-Isfahani): «bal» here serves to correct the second and nullify the first. It is as if it were said: "There is no cause here for their delusion, but their denial led them to what they committed." It has also been said: the meaning of the sentence is, "You do not remain upright in what My blessings upon you and My guidance to you require. Rather, you deny," and so on.

It has also been said that «kalla» is a rebuke against what this clause indicates of their denial of the resurrection, and «bal» is a turning away from an implied clause. It is as if it were said: "The matter is not as you claim, of denying the resurrection and the rising." Then it was said: "You are not clarified by this explanation. Rather, you deny..." and so on.

Khārijah, on the authority of Nafi', assimilated (idgham, the merging of one consonant into the next) in «rakkabaka kalla», as Abu 'Amr did in his assimilation of «al-kibar». Al-Hasan, Abu Ja'far, Shayba and Abu Bishr read «yukadhdhibūna» with the third-person prefix (yā' al-ghayba).

"And indeed, over you are watchers" (Quranic quotation: ﴿Indeed, over you are watchers﴾) is a circumstantial clause (hal) relating to the subject of ﴿you deny﴾. It serves to nullify their denial and to affirm what they deny of the recompense (jaza') in the religion, in both respects; that is: "You deny the recompense while the state is that over you, from Our side, are watchers over your deeds."

Al-Alusi's commentary on Surah 82, verses 13–16:

The saying of Him, glorified is He: ﴿Indeed, the righteous will be in bliss﴾ ﴿And indeed, the wicked will be in the Blazing Fire﴾ is a resumptive clause (isti'naf) brought to explain the outcome of the recording and writing, in terms of reward and punishment. In the indefinite form of "bliss" (na'im) and "Blazing Fire" (jahim) there is, as is not hidden, magnification and awe-inspiring effect. His words, exalted is He: ﴿They will burn therein (yasluna-ha)﴾ may be either a qualifier (sifah) of "the Blazing Fire," or a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun in "the wicked" (al-fujjar) in the predicate, or a resumptive clause built upon a question arising from the awe-inspiring description of it, as if it were said: "What is their state therein?" and so it was answered: "They will suffer its heat."

Ibn Muqsim recited yuslawna-ha (with a doubled letter, in the passive voice). ﴿On the Day of Judgment﴾: the Day of Recompense, which they used to deny, either independently or within their denial of Islam. ﴿And they will not be absent from it﴾ for an instant. The intended meaning is the continuation of the negation, not the negation of continuation, and it is like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And they will not be removed from it﴾, in indicating the perpetuity of the punishment and that they will continue to feel the Fire. It has also been said: its meaning is, "And they were not wholly absent from it before that, but they used to find its scorching heat in their graves, as the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said: 'The grave is either a garden from the gardens of Paradise, or a pit from the pits of the Fire.'"

The word "absent" (ghaibin) is in the sense of narrating a past state, and the clause has been said, on both readings, to be in the place of a circumstantial clause. But on the first it is a prospective circumstance (hal muqaddarah), and on the second it falls under the pattern of ﴿They came to you with their hearts constricted﴾. It has also been said that on the first it is a present circumstance (hal haliyyah) and not on the second, because of the separation between the burning of the Fire and the punishment of the grave on one side, and what is in the station of reckoning after resurrection on the other; rather, it is conjoined (ma'tufah) to what precedes it. The active participle may also be taken in it, namely "absent" as a present circumstance; that is, ﴿And they are not absent from it﴾ now, due to the difference of the conjoined element, which is intended to refer to the future. The discourse is according to what is known of His exalted reporting of the future in other than its form, because of its certainty. So it is not objected that some of the wicked are still among the living, and some have not yet been created in that way, and the punishment of the grave is after death; how then can "absent" be taken as a circumstance?

Al-Alusi's commentary (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on Surah 82, verses 17–18:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And what will make you know what the Day of Recompense is?﴾ ﴿Then, what will make you know what the Day of Recompense is?﴾

This is an exaltation of the matter of the Day of Recompense (yawm al-din), which they deny, following an exaltation and a expression of wonder at it, after another expression of wonder. The address in it is general, and what is meant is that the reality of its matter is such that one comprehends it with the comprehension of one who knows thoroughly (diraya dari). It has been said: the address is to the chief of those addressed, may Allah bless him and grant him peace; and it has been said: it is to the disbeliever. The use of the explicit noun in place of the pronoun is an emphasis on the awesomeness (hawl) and grandeur (fakhama) of the Day of Recompense. The discussion has already preceded concerning the verification of whether the interrogative in such a construction is a subject (mubtada') or a fronted predicate (khabar muqaddam), so do not neglect it.

Al-Alusi's commentary (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on Surah 82, verse 19:

His, the Exalted's, saying: ﴿The Day when no soul will have power for another soul at all, and the command that Day belongs to Allah.﴾ is a general explanation of the matter of the Day of Religion (yawm al-din) after its vagueness, and it conveys that its nature lies beyond the circle of knowledge (al-diraya). It has been said: this is by way of fulfilling a promise, for the negation of making one aware (al-idra') implies a gracious promise of making one aware. This is based on what is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, that he said: "Every instance in the Qur'an of His, the Mighty and Majestic's, saying ( ma adraka ) [what will make you know], He has made him aware of it; and every instance in it of His, the Mighty and Majestic's, saying ( ma yudrika ) [what would make you know], it has been concealed from him."

( Yawm ) is in the accusative by an implied verb "udhkur" (remember), as if it were said, after the magnification and arousing of desire regarding the matter of the Day of Religion, and to bring him, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him, to know it: "Remember the Day when no soul among souls will have power for another soul among souls, absolutely, not merely for the disbeliever, as narrated from Muqatil, any thing of things, etc.; for He will make you know what it is." Or it is indeclinable, built on fath, with its place in the nominative, on the view of those who hold that a time noun may be built when it is annexed to a non-declinable noun, and they are the Kufans; that is: "It is the Day when no soul will have power, etc." It has been said: it is in the accusative as an adverb of time, by an implied verb "yudanun" (they will be recompensed) or "yashtadd al-hawl" (the terror will intensify) or the like, of what the context indicates; or it is indeclinable, built on fath, with its place in the nominative, as an appositive to "yawm al-din." Both of these are not the best, since they are devoid of the meaning that the preceding words convey.

Ibn Abi Ishaq, 'Isa, Ibn Jundub, Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr read "yawmu" with a damma and without tanwin, as the predicate of an implied subject; that is: "It is a Day," not an appositive to what you have just heard. Mahbub, on the authority of Abu 'Amr, read "yawmun" with a damma and tanwin, so the clause "la tamliku" etc. is in the place of a qualifier to it, and the returning pronoun is implied; that is: "in it." "And the command" — as stated in al-Kashf — is the singular of "awamir" (commands), based on His, the Exalted's, saying: ﴿To whom belongs the dominion today?﴾, for "al-amr" is from the affair of a sovereign who is obeyed. The lam is for exclusivity: that is, the command belongs to Him, the Exalted, and not to other than Him, glory be to Him, neither as a partner nor independently; that is, all disposition is in the grip of His power, Mighty and Majestic, and nothing else. In confirming His saying: ﴿No soul will have power for another soul at all﴾, there is an indication that all are governed, obedient, occupied with their own states, subdued by their servitude to the assaults of lordship. It has been said: the singular of "umur" (affairs), meaning "shan" (matter); but this is not the case. As for Qatadah's saying, reported by 'Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn al-Mundhir: that is, there is no one who decides anything or does anything except the Lord of the Worlds, it is an explanation of the resulting meaning, not a preference for it. Moreover, his saying "alone" is not a proof, the apparent meaning is left for it, and disputing the clarity is obstinacy. In any case, there is no indication in the verse of negating intercession on the Day of Resurrection, as is not hidden. And Allah knows best.
